title: Sequence and Series – Arithmetic and Geometric Progressions
outcomes: Distinguish a sequence from a series and a finite from an infinite one; read Σ notation.
Find any term, the number of terms and the sum of an arithmetic progression, and insert arithmetic means.
Use the special sums of natural numbers, odd numbers, squares and cubes.
Find any term and the sum of a geometric progression (finite and infinite), insert geometric means and convert recurring decimals to fractions.
Sum series such as 7 + 77 + 777 + … by reducing them to a GP.
Model salary increments, instalments, depreciation and growth with AP and GP.

meta.exam_tip: Most questions are a direct use of tₙ or Sₙ. Write a, d (or r) and n first — half the errors come from using n instead of n − 1 in the general term.

concepts.title: Sequence and series
body: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers produced by a definite rule, so that for every position n there is exactly one term tₙ. 1, 4, 9, 16, … (tₙ = n²) is a sequence; a random list such as 28, 2, 25, 27 is not.
A sequence with a last term is finite; one that never ends is infinite.
A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence: t₁ + t₂ + t₃ + … . Sₙ denotes the sum of the first n terms, written compactly with the Greek capital sigma, Σ.
concepts.analogy: A sequence is a queue of numbers standing in order; a series is what you get when you add up everyone in the queue.
concepts.work: Cash-flow projections are sequences (one figure per year); the total of those cash flows is a series. Spotting the rule lets you project and total quickly.

concepts.title: Arithmetic progression (AP), its general term and arithmetic means
body: In an AP, every term after the first equals the previous term plus a fixed number d, called the common difference: a, a + d, a + 2d, … . d = any term − the term before it, and may be positive, negative or zero.
General term: tₙ = a + (n − 1)d. The n-th term from the end of an AP with last term l is l − (n − 1)d.
a, b, c are in AP if and only if 2b = a + c; b = (a + c)/2 is the arithmetic mean (AM). To insert n AMs between a and b, treat it as an AP of n + 2 terms: d = (b − a)/(n + 1).
For three unknown terms in AP, take a − d, a, a + d (four terms: a − 3d, a − d, a + d, a + 3d) — the sum then gives a immediately.
concepts.analogy: Climbing stairs of equal height: after n − 1 steps from the ground floor you have risen (n − 1) step-heights — that is why the formula has n − 1, not n.
concepts.work: Simple interest grows in an AP: each year adds the same interest. Fixed annual increments in a salary or rent agreement also form an AP.

concepts.title: Sum of the first n terms of an AP
body: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or, when the last term l is known, Sₙ = n/2 (a + l).
Proof idea: write the series forwards and backwards and add — every pair of terms adds to (a + l), and there are n pairs, so 2Sₙ = n(a + l).
If Sₙ is given as a formula in n, then tₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ (and t₁ = S₁).
When solving Sₙ for n gives two positive integer roots, both may be valid — usually because some terms are zero or because negative terms cancel positive ones.
concepts.analogy: Young Gauss added 1 to 100 by pairing 1 + 100, 2 + 99, … : 50 pairs of 101. Every AP sum is the same trick.
concepts.work: Totalling a 10-year salary or rent schedule with fixed increments takes one line with n/2 (first + last) instead of ten additions.

concepts.title: Special series
body: Sum of the first n natural numbers: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2.
Sum of the first n odd numbers: 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n².
Sum of squares: 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.
Sum of cubes: 1³ + 2³ + … + n³ = [n(n + 1)/2]² — the square of the sum of the first n natural numbers.
A series with general term like k(k + 1) or (2k − 1)² is summed by splitting it: Σk(k + 1) = Σk² + Σk.
concepts.analogy: Stack 1, 3, 5, 7 tiles in an L-shape and you always get a perfect square — that is why odd numbers add up to n².
concepts.work: The sum-of-the-years’-digits method of depreciation uses n(n + 1)/2 as its denominator — the special series in action.

concepts.title: Geometric progression (GP), its general term and geometric means
body: In a GP, every term after the first equals the previous term multiplied by a fixed non-zero number r, the common ratio: a, ar, ar², … . r = any term ÷ the term before it; r ≠ 0.
General term: tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹.
a, b, c (all non-zero) are in GP if and only if b² = ac; b = √(ac) is the geometric mean (GM) of two positive numbers. To insert n GMs between a and b: r = (b/a)^(1/(n + 1)).
For three unknown terms in GP, take a/r, a, ar — the product then gives a³ immediately.
For any two positive numbers AM ≥ GM, with equality only when the numbers are equal.
concepts.analogy: A rumour that every person passes on to 3 new people: 1, 3, 9, 27, … — each round multiplies, it does not add.
concepts.work: Compound interest, reducing-balance depreciation, inflation and constant-percentage growth in sales are all GPs.

concepts.title: Sum of a GP — finite and infinite; recurring decimals
body: Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) when r > 1, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) when r < 1 (the two forms are equal; choose the one with positive numbers). If r = 1, Sₙ = na.
Infinite GP: if −1 < r < 1, rⁿ shrinks towards 0 and S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1 the sum does not settle to a finite value.
concepts.analogy: Walk halfway to a wall, then half the remaining distance, and so on: you take infinitely many steps but never cover more than the original distance — an infinite GP with a finite sum.
concepts.work: The value of a perpetuity (a cash flow that continues forever, discounted each year) is an infinite GP — the a/(1 − r) result underlies valuation formulas you meet later.

concepts.title: Series that reduce to a GP
body: 7 + 77 + 777 + … to n terms: write each term as 7/9 × (10ᵏ − 1). The sum is 7/9 [ (10 + 10² + … + 10ⁿ) − n ] = 7/81 [10ⁿ⁺¹ − 10 − 9n].
Series such as (2 + 1) + (2² + 3) + (2³ + 5) + … are split into a GP part and an AP part, summed separately.
concepts.analogy: Like separating a mixed fruit basket into apples and oranges before counting: split the awkward series into an AP and a GP you already know how to add.
concepts.work: Breaking a messy schedule into standard pieces — a fixed part (AP) plus a growing part (GP) — is exactly how analysts model escalating contracts.

concepts.title: Applications in commerce and finance
body: AP: salary with a fixed annual increment, simple interest, straight-line depreciation (value falls by a fixed amount), recurring deposits that rise by a fixed amount.
GP: compound interest (amount = P(1 + i)ⁿ), reducing-balance depreciation (value × (1 − rate) each year), population or sales growing at a fixed percentage, instalments that double.
Always identify what one "term" means (a month? a year?) and whether the first term is at the start or end of the first period.
concepts.analogy: AP is a staircase (same step each time); GP is a snowball (grows by a percentage of its own size).
concepts.work: Checking a client's depreciation schedule, an employee loan repayment plan or a lease with escalation clauses means recognising AP or GP patterns and totalling them correctly.

illustrations.title: Finding an AP from two of its terms
illustrations.q: The 4th term of an AP is 23 and the 11th term is 58. Find the AP, its 20th term and the sum of its first 20 terms.

solution.text: t₄ = a + 3d = 23 and t₁₁ = a + 10d = 58. Subtracting: 7d = 35, so d = 5 and a = 23 − 15 = 8. The AP is 8, 13, 18, 23, … .

checks.label: common difference from t4 = 23 and t11 = 58

illustrations.title: How many terms give a required sum?
illustrations.q: How many terms of the AP 54, 51, 48, … must be taken so that their sum is 513? Explain the double answer.

solution.title: Why two answers?
solution.text: t₁₉ = 54 + 18(−3) = 0. Adding a zero term does not change the sum, so both 18 and 19 terms add up to 513.

checks.label: t19 = 0, which is why both 18 and 19 terms give 513

illustrations.title: Inserting AMs; sum of multiples in a range
illustrations.q: (a) Insert 5 arithmetic means between 7 and 43. (b) Find the sum of all numbers between 100 and 500 that are divisible by 7.

solution.text: (a) 7 and 43 with 5 means form an AP of 7 terms: 43 = 7 + 6d → d = 6. The means are 13, 19, 25, 31, 37.
(b) The first multiple of 7 above 100 is 105 and the last below 500 is 497. n = (497 − 105)/7 + 1 = 57. Sum = 57/2 × (105 + 497) = 57 × 301 = 17,157.

checks.label: number of multiples of 7 from 105 to 497

solution.text: (c) General term k(k + 1) = k² + k. Sum = Σk² + Σk = 385 + 55 = 440.

illustrations.title: Finding a GP and the number of terms
illustrations.q: The 3rd term of a GP is 24 and the 6th term is 192. Find the GP and the sum of its first 8 terms. How many terms of it add up to 762?

solution.text: ar² = 24 and ar⁵ = 192. Dividing: r³ = 8, so r = 2 and a = 24/4 = 6. The GP is 6, 12, 24, 48, … .

illustrations.title: Infinite GPs and recurring decimals
illustrations.q: Express (a) 0.454545… and (b) 0.1222… as fractions. (c) Find the sum to infinity of 8 − 4 + 2 − 1 + … .

solution.text: Check: 5/11 = 0.4545…, 11/90 = 0.1222… — always verify with a quick division.

illustrations.title: Sum of 5 + 55 + 555 + … to n terms
illustrations.q: Find the sum of n terms of 5 + 55 + 555 + … and verify your formula for n = 4.

illustrations.title: Salary, doubling instalments and depreciation
illustrations.q: (a) An executive joins at ₹30,000 a month with a rise of ₹1,500 a month every year. Find her monthly salary in the 15th year and her total earnings over 15 years. (b) A debt of ₹25,500 is repaid in 8 monthly instalments, each double the previous one. Find the first and last instalments. (c) A machine costing ₹5,00,000 is depreciated at 10% a year on the reducing balance. Find its value after 4 years and the total depreciation.

solution.text: (a) Monthly salaries form an AP: 30,000, 31,500, … . Year 15: 30,000 + 14 × 1,500 = ₹51,000. Annual totals are 12 times these, so total = 12 × 15/2 × (30,000 + 51,000) = ₹72,90,000.

checks.label: first instalment when each one doubles
machine value after 4 years at 10% WDV

jobs.title: Explaining a step-up recurring deposit to a client
jobs.role: Article assistant handling personal-finance queries for a CA firm's individual clients
jobs.situation: A client plans to save ₹2,000 in the first month and raise the deposit by ₹200 every month for two years. She wants to know the last deposit and the total she will put in (ignore interest).
steps: Recognise a fixed monthly increase: an AP with a = 2,000, d = 200, n = 24.
Explain that interest would add to this, and that the bank's maturity figure should be checked against a schedule.
jobs.takeaway: Fixed-amount step-ups are APs; total with n/2 (first + last).

jobs.title: Totalling a lease with an escalation clause
jobs.role: Junior auditor reviewing lease commitments of a retail client
jobs.situation: A shop is leased for 5 years at ₹6,00,000 for the first year, with rent rising 5% every year. The client has disclosed total commitments of ₹30,00,000 (5 × 6 lakh).
steps: A fixed percentage rise means a GP with a = 6,00,000 and r = 1.05.
The disclosed figure ignores escalation and understates the commitment; raise it with the client and correct the note.
jobs.takeaway: Percentage escalations are GPs — multiplying the first-year amount by the number of years understates the total.

checks.label: total lease rent for 5 years, 5% annual escalation

mcqs.q: The 15th term of the AP 4, 9, 14, 19, … is:
mcqs.explain: The common difference is d = 9 − 4 = 5, and the nth term is a + (n − 1)d. So t₁₅ = 4 + 14 × 5 = 74. The trap is 79, which uses 15d instead of 14d — the first term already counts as one step. In practice: an AP models anything rising by a fixed amount, such as a rent that goes up by a fixed ₹5,000 each year, and this formula gives the figure for any future year.
mcqs.topic: Arithmetic progression (AP), its general term and arithmetic means

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an arithmetic progression?
mcqs.explain: An AP has a constant difference between consecutive terms. In −7, −3, 1, 5 the difference is always +4, so it is an AP. The trap is 2, 4, 8, 16, which has a constant ratio (×2) — that makes it a GP, not an AP; 1, 4, 9, 16 and 3, 6, 10, 15 have growing differences. In practice: a loan repaid with a fixed principal each month has interest falling by a constant amount — an AP — which helps when preparing a repayment schedule.
mcqs.topic: Arithmetic progression (AP), its general term and arithmetic means

mcqs.q: The sum of the first 30 natural numbers is:
mcqs.explain: The sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n + 1)/2 = 30 × 31/2 = 465. The trap is 930, which forgets to divide by 2; 496 uses 31 × 32/2 by taking one term too many. In practice: this formula gives the sum-of-years'-digits used in some depreciation and loan-interest (rule of 78) methods, where the digits 1 to n are added.
mcqs.topic: Special series

mcqs.q: The sum of the first 25 odd natural numbers is:
mcqs.explain: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n², so for 25 terms the sum is 25² = 625. (1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, and so on.) The trap is 49, which is the 25th odd number itself, not the sum; 325 = 25 × 26/2 is the sum of the first 25 natural numbers. In practice: recognising such patterns lets an examinee answer a series MCQ in seconds instead of adding term by term.
mcqs.topic: Special series

mcqs.q: 1² + 2² + 3² + … + 12² equals:
mcqs.explain: Sum of squares = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 = 12 × 13 × 25/6 = 650. The trap is 78, which is just 1 + 2 + … + 12 (the sum of the numbers, not their squares); 6,084 = 78² confuses it with the sum-of-cubes formula. In practice: sums of squares are the building block of variance and standard deviation, which analysts compute when measuring the risk of returns.
mcqs.topic: Special series

mcqs.q: 1³ + 2³ + … + 10³ equals:
mcqs.explain: The sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the sum of the first n numbers: [n(n + 1)/2]² = 55² = 3,025. The trap is 385, which is the sum of the squares 1² + … + 10²; 55 is just the sum of the numbers. In practice: knowing these standard sums lets an analyst total patterned schedules, such as growing quantities, without writing out every term.
mcqs.topic: Special series

mcqs.q: The arithmetic mean between 18 and 46 is:
mcqs.explain: The arithmetic mean between two numbers is their average: (18 + 46)/2 = 32. Check: 18, 32, 46 is an AP with common difference 14. The trap is 28, which is the difference 46 − 18 rather than the mean; 64 forgets to halve. In practice: the AM between two price points is used for simple interpolation, such as estimating a mid-month price from opening and closing figures.
mcqs.topic: Arithmetic progression (AP), its general term and arithmetic means

mcqs.q: The geometric mean between 4 and 25 is:
mcqs.explain: The geometric mean between a and b is √(ab) = √(4 × 25) = √100 = 10. Check: 4, 10, 25 is a GP with ratio 2.5. The trap is 14.5, which is the arithmetic mean (4 + 25)/2 — a different average; 100 forgets the square root. In practice: average growth rates over periods, such as CAGR of sales, are geometric means, and using the AM overstates growth.
mcqs.topic: Geometric progression (GP), its general term and geometric means

mcqs.q: If the sum of the first n terms of a series is Sₙ = 3n² + 2n, its 10th term is:
mcqs.explain: The nth term is Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁. S₁₀ = 3(100) + 20 = 320 and S₉ = 3(81) + 18 = 261, so t₁₀ = 320 − 261 = 59 (in general tₙ = 6n − 1). The trap is 320, which is the sum of 10 terms, not the 10th term; 261 is S₉. In practice: if a cumulative total is known each month, the month's own figure is the difference between successive cumulative totals — exactly how monthly sales are read from a year-to-date report.
mcqs.topic: Sum of the first n terms of an AP

mcqs.q: How many terms are there in the AP 7, 11, 15, …, 207?
mcqs.explain: Use tₙ = a + (n − 1)d: 207 = 7 + (n − 1)4, so n − 1 = 50 and n = 51. The trap is 50, which counts the gaps between terms and forgets to add the first term. In practice: counting instalments correctly — for example, the number of EMIs between two dates — needs this '+1' care, or a schedule ends one payment short.
mcqs.topic: Arithmetic progression (AP), its general term and arithmetic means

mcqs.q: The sum of 2 + 5 + 8 + … to 20 terms is:
mcqs.explain: With a = 2, d = 3 and n = 20, Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = 10 × (4 + 57) = 610. The trap is 1,220, which forgets to divide n by 2; nearby figures like 590 come from using the wrong multiple of d. In practice: the total of a savings plan that rises by a fixed amount each month — like a recurring deposit stepped up regularly — is computed with this formula.
mcqs.topic: Sum of the first n terms of an AP

mcqs.q: The 8th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, … is:
mcqs.explain: Here a = 3 and r = 2, and tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, so t₈ = 3 × 2⁷ = 3 × 128 = 384. The trap is 768, which uses r⁸ instead of r⁷ — the first term is ar⁰. In practice: a GP models anything growing by a fixed percentage, such as a subscriber base doubling each quarter, and this formula projects any future period.
mcqs.topic: Geometric progression (GP), its general term and geometric means

mcqs.q: The 6th term of the GP 729, 243, 81, … is:
mcqs.explain: Here a = 729 and r = 243/729 = 1/3. t₆ = ar⁵ = 729 × (1/3)⁵ = 729/243 = 3. The trap is 1, which uses r⁶ (one power too many); 9 stops at r⁴. In practice: a falling GP models reducing-balance depreciation or a declining sales trend, where each period is a fixed fraction of the previous one.
mcqs.topic: Geometric progression (GP), its general term and geometric means

mcqs.q: 1 + 3 + 9 + 27 + … to 7 terms equals:
mcqs.explain: For a GP with a = 1, r = 3 and n = 7, Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) = (3⁷ − 1)/2 = 2,186/2 = 1,093. The trap is 2,187 = 3⁷, which is the 8th term (and forgets to subtract 1 and halve); 364 is the sum of only 6 terms. In practice: GP sums total any stream growing by a fixed percentage, such as the total of premiums that rise 3-fold or deposits that grow each year.
mcqs.topic: Sum of a GP — finite and infinite; recurring decimals

mcqs.q: The sum to infinity of 18 + 6 + 2 + … is:
mcqs.explain: Here a = 18 and r = 6/18 = 1/3. Since |r| < 1, the sum to infinity is S∞ = a/(1 − r) = 18/(2/3) = 27. The trap is 26, the sum of just the first three terms (18 + 6 + 2); 54 uses 1 + r in the denominator wrongly. In practice: the value of a perpetual stream that shrinks by a fixed fraction each year — like the multiplier effect of spending in economics — is a sum to infinity.
mcqs.topic: Sum of a GP — finite and infinite; recurring decimals

mcqs.q: The recurring decimal 0.777… expressed as a fraction is:
mcqs.explain: Write 0.777… as 0.7 + 0.07 + 0.007 + …, an infinite GP with a = 0.7 and r = 0.1. Sum = 0.7/(1 − 0.1) = 0.7/0.9 = 7/9. The trap is 7/10, which keeps only the first term; 77/100 keeps two terms. Any single repeating digit d gives d/9. In practice: converting recurring decimals to exact fractions avoids rounding errors in interest and ratio calculations.
mcqs.topic: Sum of a GP — finite and infinite; recurring decimals

mcqs.q: Three numbers in AP have sum 21 and product 231. The numbers are:
mcqs.explain: Take the numbers as a − d, a, a + d. Sum: 3a = 21, so a = 7. Product: 7(49 − d²) = 231, so 49 − d² = 33, d² = 16 and d = 4. The numbers are 3, 7, 11. The trap is 1, 7, 13, which has the right sum and middle term but a product of 91. In practice: the symmetric form a − d, a, a + d is a useful trick that cancels d in sums — handy for exam-speed solving.
mcqs.topic: Arithmetic progression (AP), its general term and arithmetic means

mcqs.q: Three numbers in GP have sum 26 and product 216. The numbers are:
mcqs.explain: Take the numbers as a/r, a, ar. Their product is a³ = 216, so a = 6. Then 6/r + 6 + 6r = 26 gives 3r² − 10r + 3 = 0, so r = 3 (or 1/3), giving 2, 6, 18. The trap is 3, 6, 12, which is a GP with product 216 but a sum of only 21. In practice: symmetric GP terms make products easy, just as analysts set up growth problems around a central value.
mcqs.topic: Geometric progression (GP), its general term and geometric means

mcqs.q: Three geometric means inserted between 2 and 162 are:
mcqs.explain: Inserting 3 GMs gives a 5-term GP from 2 to 162: 162 = 2r⁴, so r⁴ = 81 and r = 3. The means are 6, 18 and 54. The trap is 42, 82, 122, which are the three arithmetic means (constant difference 40). In practice: filling in intermediate values at a constant growth rate — for example, the yearly sales path between a start and an end figure — uses geometric means.
mcqs.topic: Geometric progression (GP), its general term and geometric means

mcqs.q: In a GP the sum of the first 6 terms is 28 times the sum of the first 3 terms. The common ratio is:
mcqs.explain: S₆/S₃ = (r⁶ − 1)/(r³ − 1) = r³ + 1 (since r⁶ − 1 = (r³ − 1)(r³ + 1)). So r³ + 1 = 28, r³ = 27 and r = 3. The trap is 27, which stops at r³ and forgets to take the cube root. In practice: comparing totals over two horizons to back out a growth rate is how an analyst infers the growth factor of a business from cumulative figures.
mcqs.topic: Sum of a GP — finite and infinite; recurring decimals

mcqs.q: An employee starts at ₹20,000 a month and gets a fixed rise of ₹1,000 a month every year. His monthly salary in the 10th year is:
mcqs.explain: Salaries form an AP with a = ₹20,000 and d = ₹1,000. The 10th year's salary is a + 9d = 20,000 + 9,000 = ₹29,000. The trap is ₹30,000, which adds ten increments — but the first year has no increment yet. In practice: fixed-increment pay scales, like many government and PSU pay structures, follow an AP, and HR projects future salaries this way.
mcqs.topic: Applications in commerce and finance

mcqs.q: A machine bought for ₹2,00,000 depreciates at 10% a year on the reducing balance. Its value after 3 years is:
mcqs.explain: Under the reducing-balance method values form a GP with r = 0.9: 2,00,000 × 0.9³ = ₹1,45,800 (₹1,80,000, then ₹1,62,000, then ₹1,45,800). The trap is ₹1,40,000, which deducts a fixed ₹20,000 a year as under the straight-line method (an AP). In practice: the Income-tax Act's written-down value method for depreciation works exactly on this GP pattern.
mcqs.topic: Applications in commerce and finance

mcqs.q: The sum of all two-digit numbers divisible by 3 is:
mcqs.explain: The two-digit multiples of 3 are 12, 15, …, 99. Number of terms = (99 − 12)/3 + 1 = 30. Sum = n/2 (first + last) = 15 × 111 = 1,665. The tempting near-miss totals come from miscounting the terms or starting from a one-digit multiple like 9; always fix the true first and last terms first. In practice: totalling evenly spaced amounts, such as quarterly payments that rise by a fixed sum, uses this first-plus-last shortcut.
mcqs.topic: Sum of the first n terms of an AP

mcqs.q: If a, b, c are in AP, then:
mcqs.explain: In an AP the difference is constant, so b − a = c − b, which gives 2b = a + c — the middle term is the average of its neighbours. The trap is b² = ac, which is the condition for a GP, where the middle term is the geometric mean. In practice: when three readings move by equal amounts, the middle one is their average — a quick check analysts use on evenly spaced data.
mcqs.topic: Arithmetic progression (AP), its general term and arithmetic means

mcqs.q: The AM and GM of two positive numbers are 10 and 8. The numbers are:
mcqs.explain: AM = 10 means x + y = 20; GM = 8 means xy = 64. The numbers are roots of t² − 20t + 64 = 0, i.e. 16 and 4. Check: (16 + 4)/2 = 10 and √64 = 8. The trap is 12 and 8, which gives the right AM but a GM of √96 ≈ 9.8. In practice: the gap between AM and GM measures how uneven values are, which is why average returns over volatile years overstate the compound return.
mcqs.topic: Geometric progression (GP), its general term and geometric means

mcqs.q: If 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = 210, then n is:
mcqs.explain: Set n(n + 1)/2 = 210, so n² + n − 420 = 0 = (n + 21)(n − 20). Since n is positive, n = 20. Check: 20 × 21/2 = 210. The trap is 21, the other factor (with the wrong sign); 14 and 15 come from guessing. In practice: working backwards from a known total to the number of periods — for example, how many months of a growing contribution plan reach a target — uses the same approach.
mcqs.topic: Special series

mcqs.q: The sum to infinity of 1 − 1/2 + 1/4 − 1/8 + … is:
mcqs.explain: This is an infinite GP with a = 1 and r = −1/2. Since |r| < 1, S∞ = a/(1 − r) = 1/(1 + 1/2) = 2/3. The trap is 2, which ignores the minus sign and uses r = +1/2. In practice: alternating series appear in economic models where effects reverse each round, and getting the sign of r right decides the answer.
mcqs.topic: Sum of a GP — finite and infinite; recurring decimals

mcqs.q: The 10th term from the end of the AP 3, 8, 13, …, 253 is:
mcqs.explain: Read the AP from the end: 253, 248, 243, … with d = −5. The 10th term from the end is 253 − 9 × 5 = 208. The trap is 48, which is the 10th term from the beginning; 203 uses 10 steps instead of 9. In practice: counting back from the latest figure — such as the 10th-last instalment in a schedule — uses this reversed-AP approach.
mcqs.topic: Arithmetic progression (AP), its general term and arithmetic means

mcqs.q: An AP has first term 5, last term 95 and 19 terms. Its sum is:
mcqs.explain: When the first and last terms are known, Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) = 19/2 × (5 + 95) = 19 × 50 = 950. The trap is 1,000, which multiplies by 20 terms instead of 19; 1,900 forgets to halve. In practice: totalling a stepped-up savings plan when only the first and last instalments are known uses this quick formula.
mcqs.topic: Sum of the first n terms of an AP

mcqs.q: A sum of money doubles every year under a scheme. If ₹500 is invested, the amount at the end of 6 years is:
mcqs.explain: The amount doubles every year, so it forms a GP: after n years it is 500 × 2ⁿ. After 6 years: 500 × 64 = ₹32,000. The trap is ₹16,000, which is the value after 5 years; ₹3,000 adds ₹500 a year as if growth were simple. In practice: schemes promising to 'double money every year' are a classic sign of a Ponzi fraud, and regulators like SEBI and RBI routinely warn investors about them.

viva.q: What is the difference between a sequence and a series?
viva.model: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers that follow a definite rule, so each position has one term. A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence. For example, two, four, six, eight is a sequence, while two plus four plus six plus eight is a series.

viva.q: When does an infinite geometric series have a sum, and what is it?
viva.model: An infinite GP has a finite sum only when the common ratio lies between minus one and one, that is, its absolute value is less than one. viva.q: What are the arithmetic mean and the geometric mean of two numbers, and how do they compare?
viva.model: The arithmetic mean of a and b is a plus b divided by two. The geometric mean of two positive numbers is the square root of a times b. For positive numbers the arithmetic mean is always greater than or equal to the geometric mean, and they are equal only when the two numbers are equal.

cases.title: Choosing a savings plan for an office team
cases.case: The staff welfare committee of a CA firm compares two 3-year savings plans (ignore interest). Plan A: deposit ₹1,500 in the first month and increase the deposit by ₹100 every month for 36 months. Plan B: deposit ₹30,000 in the first year and increase the yearly deposit by 20% each year for 3 years.

mcqs.q: Under Plan A, the deposit in the 36th month is:
mcqs.explain: Monthly deposits form an AP with a = ₹1,500 and d = ₹100. The 36th deposit is a + 35d = 1,500 + 3,500 = ₹5,000. The trap is ₹5,100, which adds 36 increases — but the first month has none. In practice: step-up SIPs offered by Indian mutual funds raise the instalment by a fixed amount periodically, and this formula gives the final instalment.
mcqs.topic: Arithmetic progression (AP), its general term and arithmetic means

mcqs.q: Total deposited under Plan A is:
mcqs.explain: Total = n/2 (first + last) = 36/2 × (1,500 + 5,000) = 18 × 6,500 = ₹1,17,000. The trap is ₹54,000, which is 36 × 1,500 and ignores the monthly increases; ₹1,08,000 uses a wrong average. In practice: a welfare committee or HR team totals a stepped-up contribution plan this way before comparing it with alternatives.
mcqs.topic: Sum of the first n terms of an AP

mcqs.q: Total deposited under Plan B is:
mcqs.explain: Yearly deposits form a GP with a = ₹30,000 and r = 1.2: 30,000 + 36,000 + 43,200 = 30,000 × (1.2³ − 1)/0.2 = 30,000 × 3.64 = ₹1,09,200. The trap is ₹1,08,000, which adds 20% of the first year's ₹30,000 each year (₹6,000 steps) — an AP. In practice: annual step-ups in insurance premiums or SIPs that rise by a percentage follow a GP, not an AP.
mcqs.topic: Sum of a GP — finite and infinite; recurring decimals

mcqs.q: Which plan collects more, and by how much?
mcqs.explain: Plan A collects ₹1,17,000 and Plan B ₹1,09,200, so Plan A collects more, by 1,17,000 − 1,09,200 = ₹7,800. The trap is 'Plan B', because a 20% rise sounds bigger than ₹100 a month — but A's frequent small steps add up over 36 months. In practice: a CA comparing contribution plans for an office team computes the totals rather than relying on headline percentages.
mcqs.topic: Applications in commerce and finance
